list.listitem: The clinical diagnosis of chronic sinusitis is imprecise. Computed tomography (CT) scan can be used to rule out chronic sinusitis but is not specific enough to effectively rule in chronic sinusitis. C
ENT evaluation and/or CT scan of the nasal sinuses is required to make a definitive diagnosis. C
Nasal saline washes are safe and provide symptomatic relief. B

Steroid nasal sprays are helpful for symptom relief and can be combined with saline irrigation. A In patients with chronic rhinosinusitis with polyps, nasal steroids also reduce polyp size and prevent recurrence after surgery. A
Antibiotics may be helpful for acute flares of sinusitis in patients with chronic sinusitis. C

Functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) is the currently accepted surgical treatment and may help some individuals with closed sinus ostia, but was found to be no more effective than usual medical management in a systematic review in adults. B

background.definition: According to the American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery, chronic sinusitis is symptomatic inflammation of the nasal passages and paranasal sinuses that lasts more than 12 weeks.

list.listitem: Using physicians' claims data in Alberta, Canada, the mean age- and sex-standardized incidence of diagnosed chronic rhinosinusitis was 2.5 (range 2.3-2.7) per 1000 population.
Chronic sinusitis accounts for about 2% of primary care office visits.

Authors of a systematic review of 31 studies found that patients with chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) were predominantly white (78.5%) followed by Black (7.6%) and Asian (1.2%) patients. CRS without polyps is more prevalent in females (54.2%), while CRS with polyps is found more often in males (59.8%). Allergic fungal rhinosinusitis was more common in Black patients (53.8%).

In the Canadian study noted above, the estimated prevalence, based on age-specific incidence, varied between 18.8 (95% CI, 18.7-18.9) and 23.3 (95% CI, 23.1-23.5) per 1000 population during 2004-2005 to 2013-2014.
Chronic sinusitis is thought to affect 5% to 15% of adults at some time in their lives in the United States and Europe..
Chronic sinusitis is caused by chronic bacterial and fungal infections.
The same bacterial pathogens are involved as in acute sinusitis, but also Pseudomonas aeruginosa, group A streptococcus, Staphylococcus aureus, and anaerobes.
Aspergillus sp. are the organisms most often associated with fungal sinusitis in immunocompetent and immunocompromised individuals.

In a study of 38 patients with chronic sinusitis and 6 controls, microbes were found in the sinonasal mucosa of all patients. Staphylococcus aureus and Propionibacterium acnes were the most common organisms found for all patients, but microbial abundance was associated with sinus disease.

In a systematic review of studies utilizing 16S-sequencing technology, the most common genera identified from the sinuses of patients with chronic rhinosinusitis were staphylococcus, propionibacterium, and corynebacterium.

In a review of persistent chronic sinusitis despite treatment, the authors suggest evaluation for underlying systemic causes including immunodeficiency and systemic granulomatous and eosinophilic syndromes. In a meta-analysis of case studies of chronic sinusitis, authors found a prevalence of pooled IgG, IgA, and IgM deficiencies in 13% of patients with recurrent chronic rhinosinusitis and 23% of patients with difficult-to-treat chronic rhinosinusitis. The prevalence of respiratory allergies in patients with recurrent chronic rhinosinusitis was 72%.

The cause is uncertain, but research suggests that impaired mucociliary clearance and obstruction of sinus ostia are involved in many cases. Studies have demonstrated the presence of bacterial biofilm in sinus tissue in 45% to 80% of CRS cases.

Untreated or undertreated acute sinus infections may contribute to chronic sinusitis. Alterations in the sinus mucosa biofilm may also contribute, as well as anatomic abnormalities of the nasal cavity. Nasal polyps frequently accompany chronic sinusitis.

Histologically, chronic sinusitis is a proliferative process with fibrosis of the lamina propria. There is infiltration with lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils. Bony changes and granulomas may occur.

Bacteria lysate of 21 strains of 8 bacteria administered 10 days per month for 3 months to 48 children with CRS in remission resulted in decreased nasal discharge and obstruction scores, number of days with rhinitis attacks per month, and number of days of antibiotic use per month compared to a control group of 48 children at one year.

Among patients with CRS and polyposis who were undergoing endoscopic sinus surgery, use of topical furosemide (300 µg given as 2 puffs twice daily for 2 months) reduced 6-month rhinosinusal polyposis severity based on SNOT-22 scoring compared to placebo; there were no differences, however, based on CT scan of paranasal sinuses scoring.

Diagnosis is based on the persistence of sinusitis symptoms for more than 12 weeks. Typical symptoms are facial pain, pressure, or fullness; nasal obstruction or congestion; nasal drainage or postnasal drip; and decreased sense of smell. C
No symptom or combination of symptoms has good predictive value for ruling in or ruling out chronic sinusitis. C
CT scan is sensitive for chronic sinusitis (over 90%) but not specific and should only be performed if the patient is experiencing two or more subjective symptoms. C
Consider other diagnoses if the patient is not responding to treatment. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Clear nasal discharge, sneezing, itching, seasonal flare on exposure to allergens
Absence of nasal discharge and normal CT of sinuses and positive response to migraine medication
Absence of nasal discharge and normal CT of sinuses
Positive anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody test, renal and pulmonary involvement
Acidic gastric fluid refluxes up in to the larynx and/or pharynx. Associated with heartburn, chronic throat clearing, and hoarseness

list.listitem: The American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery Foundation defines chronic rhinosinusitis as 12 weeks or longer of two or more of the following signs and symptoms: (1) mucopurulent anterior and/or posterior nasal drainage, (2) nasal obstruction (congestion), (3) facial pain, pressure, or fullness, (4) decreased sense of smell.

Inflammation must also be documented by one or more of the following findings: (1) purulent (not clear) mucus or edema in the middle meatus or ethmoid region, (2) polyps in the nasal cavity or the middle meatus, or (3) radiographic imaging showing inflammation of the paranasal sinuses.

The most common symptoms of chronic sinusitis are nasal obstruction (81%-95%), facial pain, pressure, or fullness (70%-85%); discolored nasal discharge (51%-83%); and decreased sense of smell (61%-69%). However, no single clinical finding appears to be helpful in ruling in or ruling out acute rhinosinusitis.
In one study, the number of symptoms correlated with presence or absence of disease.
In a Danish study, there was only moderate agreement between symptom reporting on a questionnaire and clinical evaluation for chronic sinusitis, with low sensitivity and high specificity.

Authors of a systematic review found that clinicians, based on their impression, were not particularly good at diagnosing rhinosinusitis or bacterial sinusitis (LR+ 3 – 4 and 2 - 6; LR- 0.3 and 0.2 - 0.5, respectively), but were at least as accurate as clinical decision rules.
Physical exam should include inspection of the nasal cavity via anterior rhinoscopy in the primary care setting and nasal endoscopy where available to rule out other diagnoses, such as nasal polyps.
Mucopurulent material emanating from the sinus meatus under the middle turbinate may be seen on nasal examination.
Deviated nasal septum, nasal polyps, and turbinate hypertrophy, and edema may be noted on examination.
Patients who report "sinus headache" or "sinus pain" are often actually suffering from migraine headaches, so always consider migraine even if patients self-report "sinus headache."
Unilateral symptoms such as nasal drainage, nasal masses, or facial pain should prompt consideration of other etiologies than chronic rhinosinusitis, such as neoplasms.

The American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery Foundation recommend CT of the paranasal sinuses for diagnosing chronic sinusitis. The American College of Radiology recommends CT without contrast for diagnosis. However, imaging should only be pursued in patients with at least 2 subjective criteria for chronic rhinosinusitis as there is a high false-positive rate of detection of sinonasal abnormalities.

Sinus CT scan was 94% sensitive and 41% specific (LR+ 1.6, LR− 0.15) in a study of 171 patients using surgical findings as the reference standard. Therefore, sinus CT is good for ruling out chronic sinusitis but less than 50% accurate for ruling it in. For example, with a pretest probability of 25%, abnormal CT increases the likelihood of chronic sinusitis to only 35%, while a negative scan reduces it to 5%.

In a study of CT imaging for diagnosis of fungus balls in CRS, preoperative CT had an 83% sensitivity and 94% specificity (LR+ 13.8, LR− 0.18); a severe inflammatory reaction of the surrounding tissue was an additional diagnostic sign.
MRI is discouraged due to increased cost and higher risk of overdiagnosis when compared to CT without contrast. Sinus plain film radiography is no longer recommended due to poor accuracy.
Diagnosis is imprecise and based on typical sinusitis signs and symptoms (see Diagnostic criteria) with duration of 12 weeks or greater.

Suspect chronic sinusitis in patients with persistent anterior or posterior mucopurulent nasal drainage, nasal obstruction, facial pressure, and decreased sense of smell. Physical or radiographic evidence of inflammation is necessary for the diagnosis, so nasal endoscopy and/or sinus CT is usually required.
Nasal saline washes can reduce symptoms. B
Nasal steroid spray is helpful for acute flares and for reducing symptoms in patients with and without polyps. A
In patients with chronic rhinosinusitis with polyps, nasal steroids also reduce polyp size and prevent recurrence after surgery. A
Antibiotics may be helpful for acute symptom flares. C
Functional endoscopic sinus surgery is no better than medical management. B

The nasal steroid fluticasone (2 puffs daily for 21 days) plus cefuroxime was more effective than cefuroxime alone in resolving clinical symptoms for flare of sinusitis in patients with chronic or recurrent sinusitis (94% vs. 74%; NNT 5).

Authors of a Cochrane review of 10 RCTs found topical steroids reduced symptoms in patients with CRS with and without polyp. In patients with CRS and polyps, nasal steroids reduce polyp size and prevent recurrence after surgery.

In a systematic review of 48 studies with 3961 patients, intranasal corticosteroids were found to be effective in reducing overall symptoms, with greater symptom improvement demonstrated in studies using direct vs. intranasal sinus delivery methods and for patients who had prior sinus surgery.

In an RCT of 80 adults with symptomatic CRS, large-volume sinus irrigation decreased symptom scores at 30 days. The addition of budesonide did not provide extra benefit; however, this small study was underpowered to prove such a difference.
There is currently no evidence to suggest that any corticosteroid spray is superior, or that increased dosage provides greater efficacy.

Antibiotics are commonly used and may be effective for acute symptom flares, but there are few RCTs of antibiotics for treatment of the more chronic symptoms of chronic sinusitis. Authors of a Cochrane review found only a single study of 64 patients demonstrating benefit with use of systemic antibiotics for the curative treatment of CRS. However, there was no difference in change in SNOT-20 score from baseline at 24 weeks between intervention and placebo groups.

High-dose clarithromycin (500 mg twice daily for 7 days then 250 mg daily for 7 days) was significantly better than low-dose therapy (250 mg once daily for 14 days) for the treatment of CRS in one RCT of 43 adults without polyps. Improvement in symptoms at 2 and 4 weeks was only seen in the high-dose group.

For nasal polyps, authors of a systematic review found evidence in support of 1 to 3 week courses of systemic corticosteroids or doxycycline (3 weeks) for reducing polyp size or use of a leukotriene antagonist for improving nasal symptoms.

In a RCT of 60 adults with symptomatic chronic sinusitis and nasal polyposis despite 2 or more months of nasal steroid therapy alone, adding subcutaneous dupilumab, a human monoclonal antibody to interleukin 4 receptor, to the treatment regimen significantly improved nasal symptom scores and reduced polyp size.
An RCT with 90 patients found that oral prednisolone and weekly intrapolyp budesonide injections were both more effective than budesonide nasal irrigation.
There is insufficient evidence for short-term oral corticosteroids as an adjunct therapy to antibiotics for CRS in adults.

Authors of a systematic review of 29 RCTs with 3461 patients evaluated 8 treatments for chronic sinusitis with nasal polyps including dupilumab, omalizumab, mepolizumab, aspirin desensitization, benralizumab, etokimab, reslizumab, and AKOO1. Of all the treatments reviewed, dupilumab, omalizumab, mepolizumab, benralizumab, and aspirin desensitization showed improvement in patient outcomes. Dupilumab was the only treatment beneficial for all outcomes that were studied.

An industry-funded RCT involving 410 adults with at least 12 months of CRS and nasal polyps compared a subcutaneous injection of the monoclonal antibody tezebelumab (210 mg every 4 weeks for 52 weeks) with placebo. At week 52, patients receiving tezebelumab showed statistically and clinically significant reductions in nasal congestion and nasal polyps severity. Additionally, the need for surgery (0.5% vs 22.1%; P < .001; NNT = 5) and systemic corticosteroids (5.2% vs 18.3%; P < .001; NNT = 8) were both significantly lower in the tezebelumab group. Adverse events were similar or less common compared to placebo. However, the monthly list price of tezebelumab is approximately US$4000, amounting to around US$48,000 for 52 weeks of treatment.

FESS is the currently accepted surgical treatment. Surgery for closed ostia re-establish the drainage pathway for the maxillary sinuses. While some patients may benefit from this procedure, there have been few studies comparing medical and surgical management of chronic sinusitis. Authors of a Cochrane review of three RCTs enrolling a total of 212 patients found FESS to be no more effective than medical management.

Authors of another Cochrane review also found no important differences between different types of surgery versus medical treatment with antibiotics and topical or systemic steroids for adults with CRS and nasal polyps; data quality was poor. It is not known whether removal of polyps alone vs. more extensive sinus surgery is the optimal treatment for these patients.
Most case series of FESS in patients failing medical treatment for CRS show improvement in most patient’s symptoms and quality of life at 1- to 7-year follow-up.

Antibiotic-soaked synthetic bioabsorbable sponges placed in the middle meatus at the time of FESS had equivalent efficacy in one RCT for controlling postoperative infections compared with conventional postoperative oral antibiotics (5.4% vs. 3.8%, respectively).
Debridement following sinus surgery did not affect disease-specific outcomes at 1 and 6 months in an RCT of 40 patients.
A randomized trial with 40 patients found that use of 1:100,000 adrenaline had no impact on bleeding or surgical field visibility.

Functional endoscopic balloon catheter dilation of paranasal sinus ostia is another technique used for chronic sinusitis. Although supported by the National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence, authors of a Cochrane review found only a single RCT showing a significant difference in favor of balloon over conventional FESS with respect to directly observed patent frontal recesses (75% vs. 63% at 1 year). An additional case series demonstrated successful in-office dilation in 69 of 74 patients with a significant mean improvement in symptoms on the Sino-Nasal Outcome Test (SNOT-20).

In an RCT of 29 patients with CRS, patients randomized to uncinectomy (removal of the uncinate process) had significant change in SNOT-20 scores at 6 months compared to those undergoing balloon sinuplasty. However, there were differences between groups in total SNOT-20 scores and there was no effect of either treatment on mucociliary clearance.
Saline nasal irrigation is effective for chronic sinusitis compared to placebo or no treatment. Nasal saline is not as effective as nasal steroids. Steam inhalation is not effective.

In a recent 4-arm RCT of 871 primary care patients in the UK with chronic or recurrent sinusitis, significantly more patients randomized to nasal irrigation, with or without steam inhalation, maintained a clinically-important improvement in the Rhinosinusitis Disability Index score compared to those randomized to usual care or steam inhalation alone (44.1% v. 36.6%) at 6 months. Steam inhalation reduced headache but had no effect on other outcomes.
Antimicrobial nasal washes have been suggested as a promising therapy, but this treatment has not been evaluated with randomized trials.
Evaluation and treatment of contributing factors, such as allergic rhinitis, may be helpful.
Consider other diagnoses in patients not responding to treatment.
A systematic review found 4 studies and no clear evidence of benefit for probiotics in patients with CRS.

Refer patients to an appropriate otolaryngologist, head and neck surgeon, if the diagnosis of chronic sinusitis is uncertain based on nasal speculum exam alone, as nasal endoscopy provides better anatomic assessment and improved visualization of muco-purulence or polyps with the added benefit of magnification.

Signs and symptoms including double vision, decreased vision, periorbital edema, ophthalmoplegia, or meningismus are suggestive of intracranial complications related to sinusitis and require immediate evaluation and treatment.
The prognosis and natural history is not adequately studied. C
Among patients with recalcitrant CRS in one observational study, there was a high prevalence of polyposis, asthma, inhalant allergy, aspirin sensitivity, and elevated disease burden. C

Olfactory dysfunction was more common for patients with olfactory cleft polyps and ethmoid opacification in one study of 418 patients with CRS. Among those with eosinophilic rhinosinusitis, asthma (OR 2.29), current smoking (OR 1.74) and age ≥50 years (OR 1.66) were additional factors associated with olfactory dysfunction.

In a retrospective study of medical therapy (4 weeks of oral antibiotics, oral steroids, topical nasal steroids, topical nasal decongestant rotation, and saline nasal irrigation), treatment was successful in 51% of 74 patients, 26 had only partial resolution and 45 patients underwent surgery. Facial pressure/pain, mucosal inflammation, and higher endoscopic severity grade were associated with medical treatment failure.
A study of 66 children with symptoms of chronic sinusitis showed a sensitivity of 86% and specificity of 85% (LR+ 5.7, LR− 0.16) for paranasal CT scan for diagnosis of chronic sinusitis.

In a large case series from a tertiary pediatric otolaryngology clinic, the 174 children with chronic sinusitis were more likely to be older (8.2 ± 4.4 years vs. 5.9 ± 4.8 years), male (63% vs. 52%), white (77% vs. 47%) and privately insured (86% vs. 56%) than the 430 children from the general pediatric otolaryngology population.

In a study of 269 children with chronic sinusitis symptoms, plain radiography by Waters' projection had 84.2% sensitivity (95% CI, 78.8-88.8) and 76.6% specificity (95% CI, 62.0-87.7) against the standard of nasal endoscopy (LR+ 3.6, LR− 0.21).
There is limited evidence of efficacy for most treatments in children as well as adults.
At least two randomized trials of saline nasal irrigation included children, and both found symptom improvement.

In an RCT in children and adolescents, ages 6 to 17 years with CRS, the addition of oral steroids for 15 days to antibiotic treatment for 30 days resulted in a clinically relevant improvement or complete resolution of symptoms more often in the intervention (steroids) vs. control (placebo) group (77.3% vs. 30.4%; NNT 2.1).

In a retrospective study of FESS in 73/115 children, 76% reported improvement in their main symptom and 71% reported improved quality of life. Improvement was less in children with cystic fibrosis, asthma/allergy, and in smokers.

In a systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 studies with 1301 children, FESS was found to be an effective treatment for chronic rhinosinusitis symptoms and improved quality of life; however, only 4 studies had Level II evidence and none had Level I supporting evidence.
